d: Read this first. These are the words the rest of the page assumes you know, each one defined before it is used to…
The moment the center gives the ball to the quarterback and the play begins.
The imaginary line running through the football before the snap. The offense and defense line up on opposite sides…
One play. The offense normally gets four downs to gain 10 yards and earn a new first down.
Where the offensive or defensive players line up before the snap.
Which types of players are on the field. Example: “11 personnel” means 1 running back, 1 tight end, and 3 wide…
The exact place a player lines up within a formation.
One offensive player moving to a new location before the snap. Teams use it to change leverage, create speed, or…
Two or more offensive players move before the snap, then stop and become set in a new formation.
The path a receiver is supposed to run on a pass play.
A group of routes or blocking rules designed to work together. A “play concept” is the idea behind the play, not…
The defense’s plan for defending receivers and areas of the field against a pass.
Each coverage defender is mainly responsible for a specific offensive player.
Defenders are mainly responsible for areas of the field and react to receivers entering those areas.
The defense sends extra rushers after the quarterback instead of using them in normal coverage.
Any pass rush that forces the quarterback to hurry, move, or change the throw. A pressure does not have to end in a…
The area close to the line of scrimmage where most run defenders line up.
A player’s positional advantage. For example, a defender with inside leverage is positioned to make inside routes…
A running lane between offensive blockers. A-gaps are closest to the center; B-gaps are farther outside.
How the defensive linemen and nearby linebackers are arranged before the snap.
A defensive back who usually lines up deeper than cornerbacks. Do not confuse the position with the two-point…
A quick way to describe the deep safety picture: one deep safety or two deep safeties.
The quarterback and running back fake a run before the quarterback tries to pass.
Run-pass option. The quarterback can hand the ball off or throw a quick pass based on what a specific defender does.
The player or area the quarterback watches to decide where the ball should go.
A short, safer pass option used when deeper routes are covered.
Football is a territory-and-possession game. The offense tries to advance the ball and score; the defense tries to…
A new set of downs, usually earned by gaining the required yardage.
One possession: every play from the moment a team gains the ball until it scores, punts, turns it over, or the half…
Six points. The ball is possessed in or carried across the opponent’s goal line.
Three points for a successful kick through the uprights.
After a touchdown, the scoring team attempts a one-point kick or a two-point offensive play.
A change of possession created by an interception, fumble recovery, or failed fourth down.
A kick used to surrender possession in exchange for field position, commonly on fourth down.
The area from the opponent’s 20-yard line to the goal line. Space compresses, so route concepts and run fits change.
Late-half offense/defense where clock preservation becomes as important as yardage.
Eleven players, three groups: the offensive line protects, the backfield handles the ball, and the receivers stretch…
Receives the snap, handles the ball on most plays, makes pre-snap adjustments, reads coverage, throws passes, and…
Primary ball carrier on many run plays. Also blocks for the quarterback, catches short passes, runs receiving…
Lead blocker / short-yardage runner in offenses that use one; less common in spread systems.
Primary outside/slot pass catcher. Runs routes, blocks on perimeter runs, stretches the defense with speed, and may…
Receiver lined up inside another receiver instead of near the sideline. This alignment gives more room to break…
Hybrid blocker/receiver. Can align inline, in the slot, out wide, or in the backfield.
Snaps the ball and usually helps set protection or blocking calls.
Interior offensive lineman. Important on inside runs, pull schemes, and pass protection.
Edge offensive lineman. Often responsible for elite pass rushers and edge-setting defenders.
A player allowed to catch a forward pass under formation and numbering rules.
Usually an offensive lineman; cannot normally be the first player to touch a forward pass beyond the line of scrimmage.
Personnel tells you who is on the field; formation tells you where they line up. The two-digit code counts running…
1 RB, 0 TE, 4 WR. Very spread-out, pass-friendly personnel.
1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR. The modern all-purpose package because it can run or pass without substituting.
1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR. Creates heavier run looks while still threatening the pass.
1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR. Heavy package for short yardage, goal line, or play-action.
2 RB, 0 TE, 3 WR. Useful for two-back formations, option football, spreading the backs out as receivers, and…
2 RB, 1 TE, 2 WR. Traditional pro-style / I-formation family.
QB stands several yards behind the center. Helps passing vision and spread run concepts.
QB is shallower than shotgun with RB directly behind. Preserves downhill run threats while keeping QB off the line.
QB takes the snap directly from the center. Helps hard play-action and traditional run timing.
One running back with no fullback. Can be under center or in shotgun.
QB under center with FB and RB stacked behind. Strong downhill run/play-action identity.
Three eligible receivers line up on the same side. This forces the defense to decide how it will cover an overloaded…
Three receivers line up close together. Their releases can cross and overlap, making it harder for defenders to…
No running back is lined up in the backfield next to or behind the quarterback. Five eligible receivers are spread…
Receivers align closer to the formation. Helps crossing routes, crack blocks, and two-way releases.
Every run is a blocking plan plus a path for the ball carrier. Zone runs block areas and let the back choose; gap…
Linemen block areas and combinations rather than a fixed defender. RB presses an interior landmark and reads the…
The line moves laterally to stretch the defense. RB reads the edge, vertical cut, or backside cutback.
Downhill run that can resemble inside zone but uses more vertical double-team concepts; RB often reads a linebacker.
Gap scheme featuring down blocks and a pulling guard leading through the intended hole.
Misdirection gap scheme. Initial action goes one way while pullers lead the ball the other way.
A defender is intentionally left unblocked at first, then hit by a pulling lineman.
Ball gets to the perimeter quickly. Success depends on edge leverage and blocking in space.
Certain blockers pin defenders inside while uncovered linemen pull around the edge.
Looks like pass protection at first, then hands the ball to a runner. Useful against aggressive pass rush.
QB reads an unblocked defender and either gives to the RB or keeps the ball.
QB attacks the edge with a pitch relationship to a back, reading the force defender.
Designed run using the quarterback as the ball carrier to gain a numerical advantage.
Fast horizontal motion receives the ball at speed to threaten the edge.
Receiver takes the ball after the initial backfield action and runs around the opposite edge.
A route is one receiver’s path. A concept combines routes so that one defender has to choose between two threats:…
Vertical route. Forces a defender to run deep and can create sideline one-on-ones.
Quick inside break. Excellent against cushion and some man leverage.
Breaks toward the sideline. Useful for timing and boundary access.
Breaks inside, usually at intermediate depth. Attacks windows between linebackers and safeties.
Receiver pushes vertical then stops or works back to the QB. Good against soft zone.
Breaks toward the goal post. Attacks middle-field leverage and split safeties.
Breaks toward the back corner. Often stresses Cover 2 or high-low concepts.
Vertical route through the inside channel. Attacks between safeties or down the hash.
Low crossing route. Great for man coverage and creating yards after catch.
Starts toward the flat then turns vertically. Creates matchup stress on linebackers or safeties.
Receiver changes the break based on defender leverage/coverage. Requires QB-WR chemistry.
Two shallow crossers intersect, creating natural traffic versus man and easy zone sits.
Three-level stretch to one side: flat, intermediate out/corner, and deep route.
Short hitch/out underneath with corner route over it. Designed to high-low a Cover-2 corner.
Short outside read combining a stick/option route, flat route, and vertical clear-out.
Multiple short routes settle in separate zone windows, giving the QB simple completions.
Multiple in-breaking routes at different depths stress linebackers horizontally and vertically.
Vertical clear route opens space for a deep dig behind linebackers.
Post plus deep dig. Can stress a single-high safety.
Four receivers attack deep seams and outside lanes, stretching deep coverage.
Deep crossing route from TE/slot with complementary vertical/flat routes.
Triangle concept with a corner route, flat route, and snag/sit route.
Two deep routes cross (a post and corner) to stress two-high safeties.
Throw behind or near the line to a runner/receiver with blockers releasing ahead.
QB rolls away from run action after a fake, usually with routes at multiple levels.
More blockers means more time, but fewer receivers. Protection is the trade-off between the two.
Only offensive linemen protect. Creates five eligible receivers but fewer blockers.
RB or TE stays in protection, reducing route count to handle pressure.
Two extra protectors stay in, typically for deep play-action or heavy pressure.
Part of the line zones/slides one way while the other side handles man rules.
Line moves in one direction to account for a pressure front; backside issues may require RB help.
Immediate route adjustment used when the offense cannot block every rusher.
Receiver/QB recognize pressure or leverage and convert the route accordingly.
RB/TE briefly hits an edge rusher before releasing into a route.
Protected area around the quarterback. Interior depth and edge width determine escape lanes.
QB tackled behind the line while attempting to pass or before escaping as a runner.
QB leaves the designed pocket after the pass play develops.
Three levels: linemen at the ball, linebackers behind them, defensive backs (cornerbacks and safeties) deepest.…
Interior defensive lineman who controls gaps, disrupts runs, and pushes the pocket.
Interior defender aligned near the center, common in odd fronts. Often absorbs double teams and controls A-gaps.
Edge or interior-edge defender depending on scheme; sets the edge, rushes the passer, and plays run contain.
Modern umbrella term for a primary outside pass rusher, whether formally a DE or outside linebacker.
Central linebacker; often involved in front checks, run fits, hook-zone coverage, and communication.
Usually faster linebacker aligned away from the strength; pursues runs and covers space.
Often aligns to the tight-end or formation strength; may set an edge, blitz, or cover.
Covers receivers, plays deep/flat zones, supports the run, and contests outside routes.
Deep safety with range; often protects the middle of the field and helps erase deep mistakes.
Safety who may play closer to the box, cover tight ends, blitz, or rotate deep depending on scheme.
Fifth defensive back, usually matched against slot receivers or used as a versatile coverage/blitz player.
Sixth defensive back, used in obvious passing situations or matchup packages.
Gaps are lettered from the center out (A, B, C, D). Techniques number where a defensive lineman lines up on a…
Space between center and guard.
Space between guard and tackle.
Space outside the tackle, often between tackle and TE if present.
Outside the tight end in heavy formations.
Defender aligned head-up over the center.
Defender shaded to one shoulder of the center.
Inside shade of the guard.
Outside shade of the guard; classic penetrating defensive tackle alignment.
Inside shade of the tackle.
Outside shoulder of offensive tackle.
Edge defender aligned very wide to attack pass-rush angle / set hard edge.
Four defensive linemen, three linebackers as the base structure.
Three defensive linemen, four linebackers, often with edge rushers standing.
Four linemen, two linebackers, five DBs. Popular versus modern spread offenses.
Three linemen, three linebackers, five DBs; flexible pressure and coverage structure.
Defensive line strength shifted toward offensive strength.
Front shifted away from strength, often creating a favorable weak-side edge alignment.
Interior covered heavily, often with a defender over center and both guards to restrict inside runs.
Defender controls blocker and is responsible for either adjacent gap based on the run.
Defender attacks a specific assigned gap.
Force a run wider so pursuit can finish it.
Keep the runner from escaping outside; turn the ball back toward help.
The number in “Cover 2 / Cover 3 / Cover 4” usually describes how many defenders are responsible for the deepest…
Man coverage with no deep safety help. Enables pressure but is vulnerable to explosive plays if anyone loses.
Man underneath with one deep middle safety. Flexible and aggressive; crossers/picks/mismatches can stress it.
One safety plays deep while another drops into an intermediate middle zone to rob in-breaking routes.
Two deep safeties; cornerbacks and underneath defenders cover flats/hooks. Classic weaknesses can include the deep…
Cover 2 variation where the middle linebacker carries vertically through the deep middle, effectively helping close…
Three deep thirds with four underneath defenders in common spot-drop versions. Strong balanced shell and common…
Pattern-match version where zone defenders convert to man-like rules based on receiver releases.
Four deep quarters. Can defend verticals well while allowing safeties to trigger aggressively based on route/run rules.
Two-high match coverage where defenders read the releases of No. 1 and No. 2 receivers and exchange responsibilities.
Quarter-quarter-half: quarters principles on one side, Cover 2 principles on the other.
Safeties can rotate down and corners take deep halves, disguising the coverage shell.
Two defenders combine to take away one dangerous receiver.
Defense sends unexpected rushers while dropping traditional linemen and playing zone behind the pressure.
Pressure is about numbers and surprise: send one more rusher than the protection can block, or rush four from places…
Zone pressure often using five rushers and three-deep / three-under coverage.
Two linebackers threaten the gaps on either side of the center, stressing protection communication.
Slot defender attacks from the edge/interior.
Safety enters the pressure, often from a disguised depth.
Shows pressure but rushes only four, replacing expected rushers with unexpected ones.
Four-man pressure using a nontraditional fourth rusher while another front player drops.
Two defensive linemen exchange rush lanes to create confusion and picks.
Rush with responsibility not to let the quarterback escape outside.
Defender mirrors a mobile quarterback rather than committing immediately to rush or zone.
Assigned gap / leverage responsibility when the offense runs.
Backside lane that opens when defenders over-pursue the initial flow.
The path a defender takes to intersect the runner rather than chase directly behind.
Use this in order. Do not try to identify the entire defense at once. Start with the easiest visual clues, then…
The same play can be smart or reckless depending on down, distance, field position, score and clock.
Entire playbook is available. Offenses value efficiency and staying ahead of the chains.
Great shot-play down because a failed deep attempt still leaves manageable third down.
Defense can anticipate pass but must respect draw/screens.
Run fits, QB sneak, quick game, picks/rubs, and compact formations become important.
Passing concepts with defined first-down landmarks matter.
Defense can play sticks coverage, pressure, or drop deep; offense often needs protection plus route depth.
No punt if offense chooses to go for it; must gain line-to-gain yardage or score.
Field is compressed. Heavy personnel, pick concepts, fades, slants, and QB run threats matter.
Sidelines, clock stops, hurry-up, spikes, timeouts, and pre-called concepts become central.
Team with lead tries to keep clock running and earn first downs.
Offense near own goal line must avoid sacks, holding, turnovers, and safeties.
Deep coverage designed to prevent explosive scores, often conceding underneath completions.
Desperation deep pass into or near end zone at end of half/game.
QB kneels to run out the clock when opponent lacks enough timeouts.
An automatic stoppage when two minutes remain in each half. It works like a free timeout for both teams.
Each kneel uses a snap plus up to 40 seconds of play clock. With no opposing timeouts, three kneels can run out…
Kicks trade possession for field position. The NFL rebuilt the kickoff in 2024 to bring returns back safely, and…
Starts each half and follows scores. Since 2024 the NFL uses the “dynamic kickoff”: the kicker is at his own 35, the…
The area between the receiving team’s goal line and 20-yard line. A kickoff must land here (or in the end zone) to…
A kickoff that goes into the end zone and is downed there. Since 2025 the ball comes out to the 35-yard line; a kick…
Return team tries to create a lane and maximize starting field position.
Returner can catch and advance unless fair catch is signaled.
Returner signals not to advance in exchange for protection after the catch.
Snapper, holder, kicker, and protection execute a timed kick.
Specialist who snaps punts and placekicks.
Fast coverage player released outside on punts.
A short kick the kicking team hopes to recover. It must be declared in advance and uses a special alignment. Since…
Special-teams formation turns into a run/pass play.
A yellow flag means a foul. Most penalties move the ball 5, 10 or 15 yards; some also award an automatic first down…
Defender is illegally beyond the neutral zone at the snap.
Offensive player makes an illegal movement simulating the start of the play.
Illegal restriction of an opponent. Offensive holding is especially common around blocks.
Illegal contact that significantly hinders an eligible receiver’s opportunity to catch a forward pass under the…
Certain prohibited defensive contact beyond the allowed area before a pass is thrown.
Illegal contact against the passer under protection rules.
Defender enters neutral zone and causes reaction/contact under rule definitions.
Offense fails to snap before the play clock expires or other delay conduct occurs.
QB throws forward pass under pressure without satisfying requirements that make the throw legal.
Serious illegal contact, usually 15 yards.
Non-football or prohibited conduct penalized by officials.
Team chooses not to accept an opponent’s penalty because the play result is better.
Qualifying fouls by both teams can cancel for enforcement purposes.
Video games reward the same logic as the real sport. Learn the thinking once and it carries across every edition.
Short side of field when ball is on a hash.
Wide side of field when ball is on a hash.
Pre-snap safety/coverage structure.
One deep safety structure.
Two deep safeties structure.
Intermediate inside zone.
Short outside area.
Outside underneath zone family.
Middle of field open, usually two-high shell shorthand.
Middle of field closed, usually one-high shell shorthand.
Extra defenders near line to stop run.
Fewer immediate run defenders.
Defender responsible for keeping the ball from escaping outside.
Each defender maintains assigned run lane.
Immediate throw replacing an unblocked rusher.
Ordered sequence of QB reads.
Run fake before pass.
Pass-pass option; concept with multiple pass choices.
QB rollout after fake.
Bootleg with little/no backside protection.
Route interaction that creates legal/near-legal traffic for defenders.
Route designed to obstruct a defender; illegal if contact rules are violated.
Initial route path before break.
How receiver begins route against leverage/press.
Tight corner alignment near line.
Corner gives cushion.
Corner opens and retreats at snap.
Physical contact at release within legal limits.
Two defenders combine on one target.
Defender jumps inside passing lanes, usually from safety depth.
Low-hole inside defender in man-free families.
Zone rules that convert based on route distribution.
Zone defenders drop to areas rather than matching releases.
Line to gain on third/fourth down.
Sideline equipment marking first-down distance.
Space defined by length of football between offense and defense pre-snap.
QB rhythm/words used to time snap.
Cadence variation intended to draw defense offside or reveal intent.
Protection identifier for the middle/declared linebacker.
Two blockers on one defender.
Two linemen block one defender then one climbs to linebacker.
Lineman leaves normal area and leads elsewhere.
Blocker tries to gain outside leverage on defender.
Blocker attacks defender aligned inside.
Receiver blocks inward on defender from outside alignment.
Back/TE/H-back blocks interior defender unexpectedly from angle.
Coverage defender blitzes when his man stays in protection.
Rusher converts to coverage if back releases.
Coordinated pass-rush lane exchange.
Broad term for defensive line movement/exchange.
Coverage player aligned wide on punt.
Ball becomes dead behind the goal line and is placed at a rule-defined spot: the 35 on kickoffs (since 2025), the 20…
Low bouncing kickoff intended to limit return setup / consume time.
Short controlled punt aimed at pinning opponent.
Where possession starts relative to the field.
The 5-yard band between the receiving team’s 30 and 35 where most of the return team lines up on a kickoff.
The yard line the offense must reach for a new first down, the yellow line on TV.
The rows of short lines (70 ft 9 in from each sideline in the NFL) that mark where the ball is placed for the next play.
A number describing exactly where a defensive lineman aligns on an offensive lineman.
Read this first. These are the words the rest of the page assumes you know.
A segment of the game in which each team gets a turn to bat. An MLB game is normally nine innings.
One of the three retirements the defense needs to end the batting team’s half-inning.
One complete turn at the plate, ending when the batter reaches base, makes an out, or another result ends the turn.
A statistical type of plate appearance. Some plate appearances, such as walks, do not count as official at-bats.
The number of balls and strikes on the current batter, written balls first: 3-1 means three balls and one strike.
The area over home plate where a pitch can be called a strike when it meets the rulebook height limits.
A pitch outside the strike zone that the batter does not swing at.
A pitch in the strike zone, a swing and miss, or most foul balls before two strikes.
A situation where a runner must advance because the batter became a runner and is pushing the runners ahead.
A runner is out when a fielder holding the ball touches the runner before the runner reaches a safe base, when no…
A batted ball that is in fair territory under the rules and remains live unless another rule stops play.
A batted ball that ends up in foul territory under the rules. Most foul balls count as a strike unless the batter…
The ball thrown by the pitcher toward home plate.
A category of pitch such as fastball, slider, curveball, or changeup, each using different speed and movement.
The group of relief pitchers who enter after the starting pitcher or in specialized late-game roles.
The pitcher who begins the game for a team.
A pitcher who enters after the starter.
A fielder used as an intermediate target so an outfielder can move the ball efficiently toward a base or home plate.
After a caught fly ball, a runner must retouch the starting base before trying to advance.
A runner tries to advance during the pitch without waiting for the batter to hit the ball.
Using a hitter or pitcher matchup based partly on handedness, because left/right matchups can affect performance.
A point scored when a runner legally touches first, second, third, and home plate in order.
Nine innings; each has a top (the visitors bat) and a bottom (the home team bats). Three outs end a half-inning.…
Batter reaches safely on fair batted ball without an error/fielder’s choice being the reason.
Four balls award first base.
Batter is struck by a pitch under applicable rules and is generally awarded first base.
Fair batted ball leaves the park in play or otherwise qualifies, allowing batter and runners to score.
Played when the game remains tied after regulation.
Every fielder has a number used in scorekeeping. A “6-4-3 double play” means shortstop to second baseman to first…
Delivers pitches, fields the center of the diamond, controls running game, and executes pickoffs.
Receives pitches, blocks balls, controls running game, communicates signs/strategy, and directs much of the defense.
Handles many throws, holds runners, and fields right side.
Middle infielder with range; turns double plays and covers bases.
Handles hard-hit balls and bunts near third; long throw across diamond.
Premium range/arm position; covers left side and anchors many double plays.
Outfielder responsible for left field; backs up throws and reads caroms.
Usually widest outfield range; often takes priority on fly balls.
Outfielder in right; often requires strong arm for throws to third/home.
Bats in lineup without playing a defensive position under DH rules.
Fielder positioned to relay throws from outfield to an appropriate base.
Moving behind a teammate/base to stop an overthrow from becoming extra bases.
The count (balls first, then strikes) is the single best summary of who is winning the at-bat. Hitters hunt in their…
Neutral count. Pitcher wants strike one; hitter decides whether to hunt a specific pitch.
Pitcher ahead. Hitter protects more of the zone and must respect chase pitches.
Hitter-favorable counts. Fastball or strike-zone predictability may rise, and hitter can hunt a location.
Balanced but hitter-friendly. Both sides can still access broad arsenals.
Battle count. Pitcher can expand; hitter must cover zone without chasing everything.
Next qualifying pitch decides walk or strikeout unless fouled off. Runners may move on the pitch in some situations.
With two strikes, hitter becomes more defensive and prioritizes contact on borderline strikes.
Taking/selecting pitches to gain information, reach hitter-favorable counts, or raise pitch count.
Attacking an early pitch because it matches a pre-planned zone/pitch expectation.
Shortening swing / expanding coverage / prioritizing contact, depending on hitter philosophy.

t: Pitch types and what they do
d: Pitches differ in speed, spin and movement. Movement is measured against a spinless ball: a four-seamer “rises” only…
Usually highest-velocity fastball, often with “ride” or less vertical drop than expected.
Fastball with more arm-side movement/sink depending on pitcher.
Fastball variant emphasizing downward and arm-side movement to generate ground balls.
Fastball-like pitch with late glove-side movement, smaller than a slider.
Breaking ball with glove-side and downward movement; speed/movement vary widely.
Slider family with pronounced horizontal glove-side movement.
Breaking ball with larger downward component and generally more speed separation than a slider.
Curve family thrown with a knuckle/finger-grip variation; not the same as a knuckleball.
Thrown with fastball arm action but lower velocity; relies on timing disruption and often arm-side fade.
Common changeup grip/type often featuring arm-side movement.
Fastball-like release that drops sharply late due to spin/velocity characteristics.
Splitter relative with deeper split grip and often more drop/lower velocity.
Very low-spin pitch with unpredictable movement; rare in modern MLB.
Very slow, high-arcing surprise pitch.
Modern hitting is measured at contact: how hard (exit velocity) and at what angle (launch angle). Hard contact in…
Putting the ball in play. Contact quality matters: weak contact can still produce outs.
Speed of the batted ball immediately after contact.
Vertical angle of the batted ball.
Statcast quality-of-contact classification combining exit velocity and launch angle.
Hit toward batter’s pull side.
Hit to the field opposite batter’s natural pull side.
Ability to drive balls into spaces between outfielders for doubles/triples.
Swinging at hittable pitches and taking pitches outside the zone.
How often a hitter swings at pitches outside the strike zone.
Share of pitches thrown in the strike zone.
Fly ball that results in a runner scoring after a catch and meets scoring criteria.
Intentional deadened contact used for placement, sacrifice, surprise, or squeeze situations.
Runner goes on pitch while batter is expected to swing/contact, opening defensive holes and protecting runner.
Runner goes, but hitter retains more discretion whether to swing.
Runners advance on hits, walks, steals and outs. Whether a runner is forced to run decides how the defense can get…
Distance a runner takes off a base before the pitch.
Additional movement as pitch reaches plate to improve reaction/start.
Runner advances during pitch without benefit of hit/error under scoring rules.
Runner is put out attempting to steal.
Pitcher/catcher throws to a base to retire or shorten a runner’s lead.
Defense traps runner between bases and exchanges throws to apply a tag.
Runner on first tries to reach third on a single, depending on ball location, speed, and arm strength.
Runner reads ball/outs and attempts to score on a single.
Fielders move closer to plate to improve chance of throwing out runner at home; increases risk of grounders getting…
Fielders reposition on almost every pitch, for the hitter, the count, the runners and the score. Since 2023 there…
Middle infielders position to turn two quickly.
First/third baseman move closer for bunt defense or runner-at-third situations.
Outfielders play deeper to prevent extra-base hits late with a lead.
Outfielders move based on hitter spray tendencies, pitch plan, and game situation.
Since 2023: when the pitch is released, all four infielders must have both feet on the infield dirt, with two on…
Relay throw is directed through a cutoff fielder to control runners and improve accuracy.
Long throw chain from outfield toward a distant base/home.
Center fielder generally has priority on many outfield fly balls; communication prevents collisions.
Non-primary fielders move behind likely throw destination to contain errors.
Corners charge; middle infield/pitcher/catcher rotate to cover bases depending on runners.
Special plays designed to control a stealing runner while preventing runner on third from scoring.
Aggressive bunt defense with corner infielders charging and middle infielders rotating.
Starters give length; relievers give leverage. Managers balance fatigue, handedness and how many times a hitter has…
Short first pitcher used strategically before bulk innings from another pitcher.
Pitcher expected to cover multiple middle innings.
High-leverage reliever used before closer, traditionally eighth inning.
Reliever commonly used to protect late leads, often in ninth.
Covers several innings when starter exits early or game goes long.
Pitcher-batter handedness can change pitch movement and platoon advantage.
Hitters often improve after seeing a pitcher multiple times; managers weigh this against bullpen quality.
Workload metric affecting fatigue and removal decisions.
Ordering pitches to alter speed, eye level, location, and hitter expectation.
Different pitches travel similarly early before separating late.
Using off-speed/breaking pitches in counts where fastball is traditionally expected.
Since 2020 a reliever must face at least three batters (or finish the half-inning) unless injured, which ended the…
There are exactly 24 base-out states: eight ways to arrange runners times zero, one or two outs. Each has a measured…
Offense values any ball in play that can score runner; defense may play in.
Offense may prioritize advancing runner; modern strategy varies by hitter quality.
Force exists at every base. Walk/HBP scores a run.
Runners can move aggressively on contact because a caught ball ends inning anyway.
Defense prioritizes preventing extra bases; bullpen leverage increases.
Managers may emphasize matchup, bullpen, pinch runners, and one-run tactics.
Bunt attempt designed specifically to score runner from third.
Defense awards first base intentionally to change matchup or create force situation.
Substitute batter used for matchup or offense; removed player cannot return under MLB rules.
Substitute runner used for speed or baserunning; replaces original player.
Better fielder enters late to protect lead.
Batter gives up likely out to advance runner; value depends heavily on context and run expectancy.
Traditional stats count events; modern stats weight them by value and adjust for ballpark and era. The first three…
Batting average: hits divided by at-bats.
On-base percentage: (hits + walks + hit-by-pitch) ÷ (at-bats + walks + hit-by-pitch + sacrifice flies).
Slugging percentage: total bases ÷ at-bats (single = 1, double = 2, triple = 3, home run = 4).
OBP + SLG; simple combined offensive measure.
League/park-adjusted OPS metric where 100 is league average.
Comprehensive run-creation rate adjusted to league/park; 100 is average.
Home runs.
Runs batted in; context-dependent counting stat.
Stolen bases.
Earned runs allowed per nine innings: earned runs × 9 ÷ innings pitched.
Walks plus hits allowed per inning pitched.
Strikeouts per nine innings.
Walks per nine innings.
Fielding Independent Pitching; estimates outcomes tied more directly to pitcher: strikeouts, walks, HBP, HR.
Wins Above Replacement estimate combining contributions into one value; implementations vary.
Batting average on balls in play, excluding HR and strikeouts from denominator structure.
Isolated power: SLG minus AVG.
